def: A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or provider interaction.
eg: The NIST definition lists five essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models; the exam expects you to reason from it, not just recite it.

def: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service (NIST). ISO/IEC 17788 names the same ideas plus multi-tenancy and scalability.
eg: If a service lacks self-service provisioning or metering, it is virtualized hosting rather than true cloud; scenario questions test that distinction.

def: Several customers (tenants) share the same physical and logical resources while the provider keeps their data and workloads logically isolated from one another.
eg: It is the economic engine of cloud and also its signature risk: a failure of isolation exposes one tenant to another.

def: The provider supplies compute, storage and networking as virtualized resources; the customer installs and manages operating systems, middleware, applications and data on top.
eg: The customer owns the most security work in IaaS: guest OS patching, network rules, identity and data protection are all theirs.

def: The provider runs the infrastructure, operating system and runtime; the customer deploys and manages only their own applications and data.
eg: Responsibility shifts up the stack, but the customer still owns application code, configuration, identities and data.

def: The provider delivers a complete application over the network; the customer configures it and supplies users and data but manages none of the underlying stack.
eg: Even in SaaS the customer always keeps accountability for their data, user access and acceptable-use settings.

def: The division of security duties between provider and customer. The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hardware, hypervisor, core services); the customer secures what they put in and how they configure it. The split moves with the service model.
eg: The most-tested concept in the domain; the safe default is that data, identities and customer-side configuration are always the customer's problem.

term: Public, private, hybrid and community cloud
def: Public: provider-owned and open to many customers. Private: dedicated to one organization. Hybrid: two or more models bound together so data and workloads can move. Community: shared by organizations with common requirements such as a regulator.
eg: Multi-cloud (several providers) is not the same as hybrid; watch for questions that test that difference.

def: Using services from two or more cloud providers, often for resilience, best-of-breed services or negotiating leverage.
eg: It multiplies skills, identity, logging and policy-consistency work, and is a stated focus of the newer CCSP outline.

term: Cloud service customer, provider, partner and broker
def: ISO/IEC 17788 roles: the customer consumes services; the provider delivers them; a partner supports either side (for example an auditor, developer or broker); a cloud service broker intermediates, aggregates or customizes services.
eg: Questions ask who bears accountability for a given duty; a broker or reseller never removes the customer's accountability.

def: An independent party that assesses a provider's controls and conformance to standards, producing assurance that customers and regulators can rely on.
eg: Customers rarely audit hyperscale providers directly; they rely on independent reports such as SOC 2 and ISO certifications.

def: A dependency on one provider's proprietary services, formats or APIs that makes moving elsewhere costly or technically hard.
eg: Mitigate with portability, open standards, exit plans and contract clauses; tested together with reversibility.

def: Portability: moving workloads or data between providers with minimal change. Interoperability: different systems working together. Reversibility: the customer can retrieve their assets and have the provider delete the rest on exit.
eg: All three are cross-cutting cloud aspects and drive exit-strategy and contract questions.

def: Scalability is the ability to handle growing load by adding capacity; elasticity is the automatic, rapid adding and releasing of capacity to match demand.
eg: Elastic implies automatic and both ways (shrink as well as grow); a manual upgrade is only scalable.

def: The provider combines its computing resources to serve many customers from a shared pool, dynamically assigning and reassigning capacity by demand.
eg: It underpins multi-tenancy; the customer typically has no control over exact physical location beyond region or zone.

def: Resource usage is monitored, controlled and reported so it can be billed and optimized, giving transparency to both sides.
eg: The same metering feeds cost-based attacks: stolen credentials used for crypto-mining show up as a spike in usage.

def: ISO/IEC 17789 lists concerns that apply across the architecture: auditability, availability, governance, interoperability, maintenance and versioning, performance, portability, privacy, regulatory, resiliency, reversibility, security and service levels.
eg: Use them as a checklist when a scenario asks what an architect must consider before adopting a service.

def: Running a workload in a private environment and overflowing to a public cloud when demand exceeds local capacity.
eg: A hybrid pattern whose risks are data exposure in the burst environment and network latency between the two.

term: Cloud security principles: defense in depth, least privilege and zero trust
def: Layer independent controls so one failure is not fatal; grant only the access required; and never trust a request because of its network location, verifying identity and context every time.
eg: Cloud has no trusted perimeter, so identity becomes the new perimeter; exam answers favor layered, identity-centric designs.

def: Protecting data while it is being processed by running workloads inside a hardware-based trusted execution environment (TEE) whose memory is encrypted and isolated even from the host and provider administrators.
eg: It closes the gap that at-rest and in-transit encryption leave open (data in use) and is named in the outline's treatment of related technologies.

term: Artificial intelligence and machine learning as cloud workloads
def: Cloud platforms provide managed training, inference and model-hosting services, so training data, models and prompts become assets that need classification, access control and provenance tracking.
eg: The newer outline weaves AI and ML security into every domain; expect shared-responsibility and data-protection angles, not deep model mathematics.

def: Processing data near where it is produced (devices, branches or local nodes) rather than in a central cloud region, to reduce latency and bandwidth.
eg: It widens the attack surface with many physically exposed nodes that need identity, patching and remote attestation.

term: Quantum computing risk and post-quantum cryptography
def: A large-scale quantum computer could break public-key algorithms such as RSA and elliptic-curve schemes, so data that must stay secret for years is exposed to harvest-now, decrypt-later collection. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in FIPS 203, 204 and 205) as the answer.
eg: Architects plan crypto agility: the ability to swap algorithms without redesigning systems.

def: A tamper-evident ledger replicated across many parties, with entries chained by cryptographic hashes. Cloud providers offer it as a managed service.
eg: It gives integrity and auditability, not confidentiality; do not store regulated personal data on an immutable ledger that cannot honor deletion.

def: Networked physical devices that sense or act, often resource-constrained and long-lived, feeding data to cloud back ends.
eg: Weak default credentials and no patch path are the usual findings; the cloud side needs device identity, certificate lifecycle and ingestion limits.

def: A vendor-neutral model (ISO/IEC 17789 and NIST SP 500-292) describing actors, activities and functional layers of cloud computing so designs and controls can be compared consistently.
eg: Use it to locate where a control belongs: user, access, services, resources or cross-cutting layer.

def: The contract component stating measurable service targets such as availability, support response and remedies when the provider misses them.
eg: SLA credits compensate cost, not business loss; resilience still needs customer-side architecture.

term: Regulator and cloud service partner roles
def: The regulator is the authority that sets and enforces legal duties on customer and provider (a data protection authority or sector supervisor). A cloud service partner supports either side; ISO/IEC 17788 sub-roles are the service developer, the auditor and the service broker, which can intermediate, aggregate or arbitrage between services.
eg: Roles describe functions, not companies: one organization can hold several. Accountability stays with the customer whichever partner is involved.

def: The technologies services are assembled from: virtualization (abstracts hardware), storage (object, volume, file), networking (virtual networks and software-defined control), databases (often multi-tenant managed services) and orchestration (automating provisioning, scaling and lifecycle).
eg: Each building block adds its own isolation and configuration risk; an architect should be able to say which block a control protects.

def: The actions each role performs in the reference architecture: the customer uses services and administers its tenancy and contract; the provider prepares, operates and secures services and manages the customer relationship; a partner audits, brokers or develops. Mapping an activity to a role shows who must perform a control.
eg: Useful when a scenario asks who should do something; the activity list is a responsibility checklist.

def: ISO/IEC 17788 classifies what the customer gets: infrastructure capabilities (provisioning compute, storage and network), platform capabilities (deploying and running customer code on the provider's runtime) and application capabilities (using the provider's software).
eg: They resemble IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, but one service can combine capability types, so analyze each capability's responsibility split.

def: Besides IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, ISO/IEC 17788 names Communications as a Service, Compute as a Service, Data Storage as a Service and Network as a Service. Container and function platforms sit between IaaS and PaaS.
eg: If a category is unfamiliar, place it by asking which layer the provider operates and which the customer still configures.

def: The Cloud Security Alliance Top Threats to Cloud Computing 2024 report lists eleven, led by misconfiguration and inadequate change control, then identity and access management and insecure interfaces and APIs, followed by weak cloud security strategy, insecure third-party resources, insecure software development, accidental disclosure, system vulnerabilities, limited visibility, unauthenticated resource sharing and advanced persistent threats.
eg: Most are customer-side failures of configuration and identity, not provider breaches; expect scenarios where the answer is governance and change control.

def: The routine basics that prevent most incidents: patching, secure baselines, hardening, immutable architecture, configuration drift detection, least privilege and removal of unused resources and credentials.
eg: Exam answers favor automated, repeatable hygiene over one-off heroics.

def: Short-lived resources such as containers, functions and autoscaled instances that are created for a task and destroyed afterwards. Attackers lose persistence and state is cleaned up, but evidence disappears with the resource unless logs and snapshots are shipped out first.
eg: Pair ephemeral designs with centralized logging and automated forensic capture.

def: Controls that limit where resources can be created or from where they can be reached, such as policies allowing only approved regions or blocking access from unapproved countries using IP geolocation.
eg: Supports residency rules, but IP geolocation can be spoofed, so combine it with identity controls.

def: Examining packets or flows with firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention, web application firewalls or inspecting proxies, using virtual appliances, traffic mirroring or provider-native services because physical choke points no longer exist.
eg: Encrypted traffic needs termination at an inspection point or metadata analysis; the choice trades visibility against privacy and latency.

term: Cost-benefit analysis and return on investment (ROI)
def: Weighing the full cost of a control or migration (licenses, labor, risk) against its benefit (loss avoided, savings). The ROI is gain minus cost, divided by cost. A safeguard is justified when the annual loss it prevents exceeds its annual cost.
prompt: Weighing the full cost of a control or migration (licenses, labor, risk) against its benefit (loss avoided, savings). The _____ is gain minus cost, divided by cost. A safeguard is justified when the annual loss it prevents exceeds its annual cost.
eg: These numbers feed the business impact analysis and the decision on which recovery or control option to fund.

def: Security-related capabilities a cloud design must provide, including portability, interoperability, vendor lock-in limits, encryption, identity integration, logging and the ability to exit, derived from business needs and regulation.
eg: Write them before choosing a provider so the evaluation tests the requirement rather than the sales pitch.

term: Secure design principles and cloud design patterns
def: Classic principles such as least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, separation of duties, economy of mechanism and defense in depth guide architecture, as taught in SANS and similar guidance. Patterns apply them, for example landing zones, hub-and-spoke networks and private endpoints.
eg: When a question asks which design is best, pick the one that applies these principles by default instead of relying on later hardening.

def: Provider design guidance organized into pillars. AWS Well-Architected has six: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. Azure Well-Architected has five and omits sustainability as a pillar.
eg: Treat them as review checklists; the exam cares that security is one pillar balanced against the others, not the vendor details.

def: A Cloud Security Alliance reference architecture, methodology and assessment tool for designing and evaluating security architecture across business operations, IT operations, information technology and security and risk management, building on established methods such as SABSA and TOGAF.
eg: Use it to compare a provider's offering with your own required security capabilities.

term: Secure by design and secure by default
def: Secure by design builds security into architecture from the start through early threat modeling and a small attack surface. Secure by default ships services with safe settings (private, encrypted, least privilege) so customers need no extra hardening to be safe.
eg: Public-by-default storage or open management ports are the textbook counterexamples.

term: Data science and big data in the cloud
def: Analytics and machine learning platforms that gather large datasets from many sources. Risks include aggregating sensitive data in one lake, re-identification by joining datasets, credentials embedded in notebooks and uncontrolled copies of extracts.
eg: Apply classification, minimization and fine-grained access before data enters the platform, not after.

def: Verify the provider against defined criteria: certifications and audit reports (ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2, CSA STAR), control mapping to a framework such as the CCM, data location and residency, key and encryption options, incident transparency, SLA terms, financial viability and exit provisions.
eg: Define the criteria first, then collect evidence; certificates prove a scope, not suitability for your workload.

def: An international standard for evaluating the security of IT products against a security target, with results expressed as an evaluation assurance level from EAL1 to EAL7 and recognized across participating countries.
eg: It evaluates products, so a Common Criteria certified hypervisor does not certify the cloud service built on it.

def: FIPS 140 sets security requirements for cryptographic modules at four levels. FIPS 140-3 (2019) supersedes 140-2; after September 21, 2026, modules validated under 140-2 move to the Historical list and may be used only in existing systems.
eg: The outline still names 140-2; know both, and remember that validation applies to a specific module and version.

term: AI and ML for cloud threat detection and analysis
def: Machine learning models learn normal behavior to flag anomalies in logs, identity activity and network flows, and can cluster alerts and prioritize them. Models need quality training data, tuning for false positives and human review of consequential actions.
eg: AI augments analysts; an automated block based on an unvalidated model is a risk in its own right.

term: Data source validation and verification for AI
def: Checking that data feeding a model comes from trusted, authorized sources (validation) and that it is accurate, complete and unaltered (verification), using provenance records, hashes, schema and outlier checks.
eg: Untrusted or unverified inputs are the entry point for data poisoning.

def: Bias and unfair outcomes, lack of transparency and explainability, privacy intrusion, unclear accountability for automated decisions, and misuse such as deepfakes. Controls include diverse and reviewed data, human oversight, documentation and impact assessments.
eg: A security professional raises these as risks that need an owner, not as abstract philosophy.

def: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) takes a risk-based approach with unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk tiers. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 organizes AI risk work into govern, map, measure and manage. ISO/IEC 42001 defines an AI management system.
eg: Know the structure of each, not the dates; the exam asks which approach fits a scenario.

def: Create, store, use, share, archive and destroy: the six phases data passes through, each needing its own controls and ownership. Data can move between phases in any direction over time.
eg: Tests ask which control fits which phase, for example classification at create and verified destruction at the end.

def: Labeling data by sensitivity and business impact (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so that handling, encryption, access and retention rules can be applied consistently.
eg: Classification is the first step; without it every later control is a guess. The data owner assigns it.

def: Finding where sensitive data actually lives, using content inspection, pattern matching, labels and machine learning, across structured, unstructured and semi-structured stores.
eg: Cloud sprawl and shadow IT mean you cannot protect what you have not found; discovery precedes classification and DLP.

def: The owner is accountable for the data and decides classification and access; the steward manages quality and rules day to day; the custodian operates the systems that hold it. In cloud the provider is typically a custodian or processor.
eg: Accountability cannot be delegated to the provider even though custody can.

def: The controller decides why and how personal data is processed and carries primary legal responsibility; the processor handles it on the controller's behalf under contract.
eg: In most cloud scenarios the customer is the controller and the provider is the processor; sub-processors extend the chain.

def: Structured data fits a fixed schema (relational tables); unstructured has no model (documents, images, email); semi-structured carries tags but no rigid schema (JSON, XML).
eg: Discovery and DLP are hardest on unstructured data, which is most of what organizations hold.

def: Controls that discover, monitor and block the unauthorized movement of sensitive data across endpoints, networks and cloud services, using content and context rules.
eg: DLP depends on classification and discovery; encrypted traffic needs inspection points that can see the content.

def: Persistent protection that travels with a file, enforcing who may open, copy, print or forward it, and allowing access to be revoked after sharing.
eg: Best answer when the requirement is control of a document after it leaves your environment; DLP only controls egress.

def: Rules for how long each class of data must be kept and when it must be disposed of, driven by legal, regulatory and business needs.
eg: Keep too little and you violate law; keep too much and you enlarge breach and eDiscovery exposure.

def: A directive suspending normal deletion of data that may be relevant to litigation or investigation until counsel releases it.
eg: Overrides retention schedules; cloud lifecycle and auto-delete rules must be able to honor it.

def: Because customers cannot physically destroy provider media, cloud destruction relies on cryptographic erasure: encrypt the data and destroy every copy of the key, rendering the data unrecoverable.
eg: The standard cloud answer to 'how do you guarantee deletion'; it works only if keys are truly isolated and destroyed.

def: Breaking data into fragments and spreading them across multiple locations or providers (as erasure coding does) so no single location holds usable data and availability improves.
eg: Improves durability and resilience but complicates data residency and deletion tracking.

term: Data flows and data flow diagrams
def: A map of where data enters, moves, is processed, stored and leaves a system, including across providers and regions.
eg: Required to find trust boundaries, apply residency rules and answer regulator questions; a first step in cloud risk work.

term: Data lake and AI training dataset security
def: Large central repositories and curated datasets used for analytics and model training need classification, fine-grained access control, lineage tracking and protection against tampering, since poisoned data corrupts every model trained on it.
eg: Newer outline content: integrity and provenance of training data matter as much as confidentiality.

def: Replacing sensitive values with realistic but non-sensitive ones (static masking in copies, dynamic masking at query time) so non-production use does not expose real data.
eg: Masking can be irreversible, unlike tokenization; the best test-data answer when real values are not needed.

def: Anonymization irreversibly removes the link to an individual so data is no longer personal data; pseudonymization replaces identifiers with a separate key or mapping, so data remains personal data under privacy law.
eg: Pseudonymized data is still regulated under GDPR; truly anonymized data is not. Re-identification risk is the tested trap.

def: Attaching metadata such as classification, owner and retention class to data and cloud resources so policies and automation can act on them.
eg: Labels make DLP, access policy and billing work at scale; unlabeled assets are the gap attackers and auditors find.

def: Object storage holds data as objects with metadata over APIs; block storage provides raw volumes for VMs and databases; file storage offers shared file systems. Ephemeral storage disappears with the instance.
eg: Each type has different encryption, access and exposure risks; public object buckets are the classic misconfiguration.

def: Tools that observe database queries and changes in real time, flagging or blocking suspicious access and producing audit trails independent of the database's own logs.
eg: A detective control for privileged-user abuse; useful where native logging is limited or tamper-prone.

term: Encryption at rest, in transit and in use
def: At rest protects stored data, in transit protects data crossing a network (for example TLS) and in use protects data while processed (confidential computing). A complete strategy covers all three.
eg: Pick the answer that matches the state of data in the scenario; one control rarely covers all three.

def: Symmetric uses one shared secret key and is fast, suiting bulk data; asymmetric uses a public and private key pair and is slower, suiting key exchange, signatures and identity.
eg: Real systems combine them: asymmetric to exchange or wrap a symmetric key that protects the bulk data.

def: A data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the data; a key encryption key (KEK) held in a key management service encrypts the DEK. Rotating or revoking the KEK controls many DEKs cheaply.
eg: The default design in cloud storage and database services; crypto-shredding works by destroying the KEK.

def: A managed service that creates, stores, rotates, controls access to and audits use of cryptographic keys, integrated with the provider's other services.
eg: Convenient and the default, but the provider operates it unless you add stronger options such as BYOK or HYOK.

def: A tamper-resistant device that generates and stores keys and performs cryptographic operations without exposing the keys; validated to standards such as FIPS 140.
eg: Choose an HSM (or cloud HSM) when policy demands hardware-protected, single-tenant key custody.

def: The customer generates the key material and imports it into the provider's KMS or HSM, keeping an original copy and the ability to revoke or delete it.
eg: More control than provider-generated keys, but the provider still uses the key to decrypt on your behalf.

def: The customer keeps keys entirely outside the provider, for example in an on-premises HSM, so the provider can never decrypt the data and services that need plaintext may not work.
eg: Strongest separation of duties, with trade-offs in availability, latency and feature support.

def: Generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, archival and destruction. Weakness at any stage undermines the encryption built on the key.
eg: Know the order and the control at each step; poorly protected key storage and absent rotation are the common failures.

def: Keys should be stored apart from the data they protect and managed by different administrators than the data owners; escrow places a copy with a trusted third party for recovery.
eg: Storing keys beside data in the same account defeats encryption; escrow introduces its own exposure that must be justified.

def: Substituting sensitive data with a random surrogate token while the real value sits in a secured vault; the token has no mathematical relationship to the original.
eg: Reduces compliance scope (for example for card data) because systems holding only tokens never touch the real value.

def: A hash is a one-way fixed-length fingerprint for integrity checks; a digital signature signs a hash with a private key to prove origin, integrity and non-repudiation.
eg: Hashing is not encryption and is not reversible; salted hashes protect stored passwords.

def: The protocol that provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication for data in transit using certificates; TLS 1.3 is the current version and removes legacy weaknesses.
prompt: The protocol that provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication for data in transit using certificates; _____ 1.3 is the current version and removes legacy weaknesses.
eg: Prefer TLS 1.2 or higher with strong suites; disable legacy SSL and early TLS.

term: Public key infrastructure (PKI) and certificate lifecycle
def: The roles, policies and services (certificate authorities, registration, revocation) that bind public keys to identities and manage certificates from issuance to expiry.
eg: Expired or unrevoked certificates cause outages and exposure; automate renewal and monitor transparency logs.

def: Encryption that allows computation directly on ciphertext, yielding an encrypted result that decrypts to the correct output, so data stays protected while processed.
eg: Powerful but computationally expensive; an answer for data in use when enclaves are not acceptable.

def: Designing systems so cryptographic algorithms, key lengths and libraries can be replaced quickly without redesigning applications.
eg: Directly addresses post-quantum migration and deprecated algorithm risk.

def: Provider-managed keys are created, rotated and held by the provider by default; customer-managed keys are controlled by the customer in KMS or HSM with their own policies, rotation and revocation, while the provider's service still performs the cryptography.
eg: Customer-managed keys mean the customer controls revocation; they are not the same as HYOK.

def: Central storage, rotation and audited access for non-human credentials such as API keys, passwords and certificates, injected at runtime rather than embedded in code or images.
eg: Hard-coded secrets in repositories and container images are among the most frequent real-world cloud breaches.

term: Media sanitization levels: clear, purge and destroy
def: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 groups sanitization into clear (logical techniques such as overwriting that defeat simple recovery), purge (makes recovery infeasible even with laboratory techniques, including cryptographic erase) and destroy (physically ruining the media).
eg: Customers cannot destroy provider hardware, so in the cloud the realistic choices are overwriting where it is verifiable and cryptographic erase.

term: Overwriting and its limits in the cloud
def: Overwriting writes patterns over stored data. On solid-state drives with wear leveling, and on virtualized or replicated storage, the customer cannot be sure every physical copy was overwritten, so overwriting alone gives weak assurance.
eg: Cryptographic erase sidesteps the problem, which is why it is the preferred answer for sanitization in shared storage.

def: Volume (block) storage attaches to an instance as a disk the customer's operating system formats. Raw storage maps a device or logical unit directly to a virtual machine, bypassing the file-system abstraction. Long-term (archive) storage is cheap with slow retrieval and often offers immutability settings. Ephemeral storage vanishes with the instance.
eg: Match the type to the requirement: durable and shared, high performance, or cheap and rarely read, and encrypt each according to its exposure.

def: Misconfigured permissions and public buckets, leaked access keys, shared snapshots, data remanence after reallocation, weak or absent encryption, ransomware that deletes versions and backups, insider access at the provider and silent data corruption.
eg: Controls that map to these: private by default, encryption with customer keys, versioning and object lock, access logging and integrity checks.

def: Tooling that continuously discovers data stores across cloud accounts, classifies their content, maps who and what can reach them and flags exposure, so data location and risk stay current.
eg: It automates discovery and the data-location question; it does not replace DLP or encryption.

def: Structured data is found through schemas and column scans; unstructured files need content inspection, pattern matching, OCR and machine-learning classifiers; semi-structured formats such as JSON, XML and logs are parsed for keys and values. Location comes from inventory, tags and scans.
eg: Each type needs a different technique, so one scanner rarely covers an estate.

def: Documenting each data element with its source, systems, owner, purpose, location, recipients and legal basis. It is the foundation for data flow diagrams, residency decisions and the records of processing that privacy law expects.
eg: Mapping answers where data is; classification answers how sensitive it is; both are needed.

def: A policy that defines classification levels, who assigns them, the handling rules for each (storage, encryption, sharing, retention and disposal), and when labels are reviewed or downgraded.
eg: A policy without handling rules per level is only a labeling exercise.

term: IRM objectives: rights, provisioning and access models
def: Data rights define what a recipient may do (view, edit, print, copy, forward, expire). Provisioning is how rights are issued and bound to users or groups. Access models decide who qualifies, such as roles, attributes or policy conditions like time and location.
eg: IRM extends access control beyond the first opening of the file.

def: IRM relies on a policy server, client agents or plug-ins, and certificates or licenses that are issued to authorized users and revoked when access ends. Challenges include slow revocation for offline copies, format support, screen capture and key distribution.
eg: Revocation only works when the client checks back with the policy server.

def: Static masking creates a permanently altered copy; dynamic masking hides values at query time by role. Other techniques are substitution, shuffling, nulling, randomization, generalization and format-preserving tokens. Anonymization combines such steps until individuals cannot be re-identified.
eg: Pick static masking for test copies and dynamic masking for production views.

def: Archive in formats that remain readable for the whole retention period, plan for media and software obsolescence, protect integrity with hashes or immutable storage, keep decryption keys as long as the data, index for retrieval and test restores.
eg: An archive whose key was destroyed or whose format cannot be opened is a deletion by accident.

def: Deletion can be logical (marking data removed), overwriting, cryptographic erase or physical destruction by the provider. A real procedure also covers replicas, snapshots and backups, records proof of deletion and respects legal holds.
eg: Ask the provider for deletion evidence in the contract, because customers cannot witness destruction.

def: A hold places relevant data in preservation by suspending lifecycle deletion and enabling retention locks, restricts access to authorized custodians, extends to backups and SaaS data, and ends only when counsel releases it.
eg: Document scope, custodians and release; a hold that silently fails is spoliation.

def: Data events come from the management plane, identity provider, storage and database access, network flows, applications and endpoints. Useful attributes are who (identity), what action, when (synchronized time), where (IP address, geolocation, resource) and the outcome.
eg: An event missing identity or reliable time cannot support accountability or forensics.

def: Auditability is the ability to examine records and controls; traceability is following an action or data item from origin through its handling; accountability is attributing each action to a responsible identity who cannot plausibly deny it.
eg: They depend on unique identities, protected logs and time synchronization.

def: Assurance that an actor cannot credibly deny an action, achieved with digital signatures made by a private key only the actor holds, trusted timestamps, tamper-evident logs, unique accounts and documented chain of custody.
eg: Shared accounts destroy non-repudiation however good the logging is.

def: Protect training data and prompts with minimization, redaction, access control and retention limits. Techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning reduce disclosure; models can memorize data, so membership inference and training-data extraction are privacy risks.
eg: Personal data used for training stays subject to privacy law even when it ends up inside weights.

def: Validate and verify datasets with provenance records, hashes and outlier checks to catch poisoning, and verify model artifacts with signing and scanning, including for unsafe serialization formats. Restrict the model registry, since weights are valuable intellectual property.
eg: Treat a model file like executable code from a supply chain.

def: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware and underpins cloud platforms; a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on a host operating system and is mostly used on workstations.
eg: A hypervisor compromise exposes every guest on the host, so hardening and patching it is the provider's top priority.

def: An attack in which code inside a guest virtual machine breaks isolation and reaches the hypervisor or other guests.
eg: The canonical multi-tenancy threat; mitigations are patching, minimal hypervisor features and placing very sensitive workloads on dedicated hosts.

def: Shared hardware lets one tenant infer secrets from another through timing, cache or resource-contention effects, or degrade a neighbor's performance by consuming shared resources.
eg: Mitigate with dedicated hosts, resource quotas and confidential computing for the most sensitive workloads.

def: Containers share the host kernel and are separated by namespaces and control groups; this is lighter than a virtual machine but a weaker isolation boundary.
eg: A kernel flaw can affect every container on the host; sensitive multi-tenant workloads may need VM-level isolation.

def: Build images from trusted minimal base images, scan for vulnerabilities and embedded secrets, sign them and pull only from a trusted registry, and rebuild rather than patching running containers.
eg: Shift-left scanning plus admission control that refuses unsigned or vulnerable images is the standard answer.

def: Role-based access control for the API server, network policies between pods, pod security standards, secrets protection, admission controllers and an audit log of control-plane activity.
eg: The control plane and kubelet APIs are the crown jewels; an exposed dashboard or over-privileged service account is the usual breach.

def: Code runs in short-lived, provider-managed execution environments triggered by events, with no servers for the customer to patch.
eg: Risks shift to over-privileged function roles, insecure event inputs, vulnerable dependencies and poor visibility; apply least privilege per function.

def: A logically isolated virtual network in a public cloud, divided into subnets (public or private) with route tables controlling whether traffic can reach the internet.
eg: Place data tiers in private subnets with no direct internet route; public exposure should be a deliberate exception.

def: Security groups are stateful rules attached to instances or interfaces; network access control lists are stateless rules applied at the subnet boundary and evaluated in order.
eg: Stateful means return traffic is allowed automatically; stateless rules need both directions defined.

def: Applying fine-grained policy between individual workloads or tiers so a compromised host cannot move freely to its neighbors.
eg: The cloud answer to lateral movement; it replaces coarse network zones with identity- or tag-based rules.

def: Separating the network control plane from the data plane so networks are configured programmatically through APIs rather than device by device.
eg: Enables automation and consistent policy but makes the management API a high-value target.

def: Granting access to specific applications per session based on verified user, device and context, instead of placing users on a broad network through a traditional VPN.
eg: Preferred over network-level VPN access for remote users when the stem stresses least privilege.

def: Dedicated links or VPN tunnels join on-premises networks to the cloud, and private endpoints expose a cloud service on a private address so traffic never traverses the public internet.
eg: A dedicated link is private but not automatically encrypted; add encryption if the data requires it.

def: Provider and third-party services absorb or scrub volumetric and application-layer floods using large capacity, anycast routing and rate limiting.
eg: Elasticity helps, but unmetered scaling during an attack can become an economic denial of service; set budgets and alerts.

def: Servers and containers are never modified after deployment; changes are made by building a new image and replacing the old instances.
eg: Removes configuration drift and makes rollback and forensics simpler; patching means redeploying.

def: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled templates that are reviewed, scanned for misconfiguration and enforced with policy as code before deployment.
eg: A misconfigured template replicates a flaw at scale; scanning in the pipeline is cheaper than finding it in production.

def: A trusted platform module and secure or measured boot verify the integrity of firmware and boot components, and remote attestation lets a service confirm a host's state before trusting it.
eg: Underpins confidential computing and trustworthy workload placement.

def: Resilient facilities use redundant power, cooling and connectivity (for example N+1 or 2N), physical access control and environmental monitoring, and are evaluated against recognized tier or standards frameworks.
eg: Customers cannot inspect hyperscale sites, so they rely on independent audit reports and certification evidence.

def: The console, APIs and command-line tools used to create, configure and delete cloud resources.
eg: Compromise of management-plane credentials is catastrophic; protect it with multi-factor authentication, least privilege and detailed audit logging.

term: Business continuity, disaster recovery and BCDR planning
def: Business continuity keeps critical functions running through disruption; disaster recovery restores IT systems after a disaster; BCDR planning addresses both together.
eg: DR is a subset of continuity; start from business impact analysis, not from technology.

def: A structured assessment of how the loss of each process affects the organization over time, producing criticality rankings and recovery targets.
eg: Recovery objectives must come from the BIA; choosing technology first is a classic wrong answer.

def: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage.
eg: A smaller RTO demands more expensive, more automated recovery options.

def: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, determining how often data must be replicated or backed up.
eg: RPO drives backup and replication frequency; RTO drives the recovery architecture.

def: The longest an organization can lose a function before the harm becomes unacceptable, which sets an upper bound above the RTO.
eg: RTO must be shorter than the maximum tolerable downtime or recovery will arrive too late.

def: A region is a geographic area; availability zones are isolated data-center groups within it. Spreading across zones tolerates a facility failure, spreading across regions tolerates a regional disaster.
eg: Match the design to the failure scenario and to data residency constraints.

def: In increasing cost and speed: backup and restore, pilot light (minimal core running), warm standby (scaled-down copy) and active-active (full capacity in more than one location).
eg: Pick the cheapest option that meets the stated RTO and RPO.

def: Synchronous replication commits to both sites before acknowledging, giving near-zero data loss but adding latency; asynchronous acknowledges first and copies later, performing better over distance but risking some data loss.
eg: A near-zero RPO across long distances usually conflicts with performance; know the trade-off.

def: Backups that cannot be altered or deleted for a retention period, or are logically separated from production credentials, so ransomware or an attacker cannot destroy them.
eg: The key defense against ransomware; test restores, not just backups.

def: Identifying assets, threats and vulnerabilities in a cloud design, estimating likelihood and impact and choosing treatment. Typical cloud risks include loss of governance, isolation failure, insecure interfaces, management-plane compromise and vendor lock-in.
eg: Risk analysis precedes control selection, and the owner of the asset accepts residual risk.

def: Deliberately injecting failures, from game-day exercises to automated experiments, to confirm that failover, alerting and recovery procedures really work.
eg: An untested plan is an assumption; tabletop, simulation and full failover tests are increasing in realism and risk.

def: The physical environment (facilities, power, cooling), network and communications, compute, virtualization, storage and the management plane. Each layer has its own owner and controls, and the management plane governs all the rest.
eg: A complete risk review walks through all six layers and assigns each to the provider or the customer.

term: Logical data center design: tenant partitioning
def: Separating tenants logically with virtual networks, distinct accounts or subscriptions, per-tenant encryption keys and role-based access, so a mistake or compromise in one tenant cannot reach another. Dedicated hosts add physical separation where required.
eg: Partitioning is the logical answer to multi-tenancy; isolation evidence comes from the provider's audit reports.

term: Physical data center design: location and buy or build
def: Site choice weighs natural hazards, power and connectivity, political and legal climate, distance between sites and proximity to users. The buy, build or lease decision trades cost and control against speed and the ability to prove controls to auditors.
eg: Customers of public cloud rarely choose; they verify through reports and region selection.

term: Environmental design: HVAC, fire suppression and pathways
def: Cooling uses hot and cold aisle layouts and sensors, with ASHRAE recommending roughly 18 to 27 degrees Celsius at server inlets. Fire protection uses detection plus clean-agent or pre-action systems. Multi-vendor pathway connectivity means carriers enter by physically separate routes.
eg: Redundant carriers sharing one trench still share one failure point.

def: The Uptime Institute rates sites from Tier I (basic capacity, commonly cited at 99.671 percent availability) through Tier II (99.741), Tier III (concurrently maintainable, 99.982) to Tier IV (fault tolerant, 99.995). Standards such as TIA-942 and ISO/IEC 22237 also describe facility design.
eg: Higher tiers mean redundant paths for power and cooling and the ability to maintain without downtime.

def: Uninterruptible power supplies bridge outages until generators start; N+1 adds one spare unit, 2N duplicates the whole path. Resilient sites also use multiple carriers, redundant cooling and tested failover.
eg: Untested generators and shared fuel contracts are classic single points of failure.

term: Quantitative risk analysis: SLE, ARO and ALE
def: Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor; annualized rate of occurrence is how often per year; annualized loss expectancy is SLE times ARO. A safeguard is worthwhile when the reduction in ALE exceeds its annual cost.
eg: Qualitative analysis ranks risks high, medium or low when numbers are unreliable.

def: Qualitative assessment rates likelihood and impact on scales and is fast and subjective. Quantitative assessment uses monetary values and probabilities and supports cost-benefit decisions but needs good data. Many programs combine them.
eg: Choose by the decision: ranking a backlog needs qualitative; funding a control needs numbers.

def: A server-side request forgery flaw can make a workload fetch its own metadata service address and return temporary credentials for its role. Mitigations include the session-token version of the metadata service, least-privilege roles, egress filtering and input validation.
eg: The attack turns an application bug into cloud account access, so role scope matters.

def: Account and credential hijacking, cryptojacking of stolen compute, exposed management interfaces, cross-tenant side-channel and escape attempts, volumetric denial of service and denial of wallet, where abuse inflates the metered bill.
eg: Detection ties to metering and baseline anomalies; prevention to identity and network controls.

def: Controls at the facility: perimeter and badge access, mantraps, cameras, visitor logs, locked cages, environmental sensors, fire suppression and secure equipment disposal. In the cloud the provider operates them and customers verify through reports; on-premises components stay the customer's task.
eg: Hybrid designs leave the customer responsible for the physical controls of its own site.

def: Protective controls for the technical stack: hardened and patched hosts, encrypted storage with managed keys, encrypted network paths, segmentation, boundary protection and denial-of-service defense, applied through policy as code.
eg: Frameworks such as NIST SP 800-53 group these as system and communications protection controls.

term: Audit mechanisms: log collection, correlation and packet capture
def: Collect management-plane, identity, flow and workload logs centrally, correlate events across sources to see attack chains, and use traffic mirroring or virtual taps for packet capture when content-level evidence is needed.
eg: Packet capture is costly and privacy-sensitive; reserve it for targeted investigations.

def: The percentage of normal service capacity that must be available during recovery, for example running at half capacity after failover. It lets planners provision a smaller recovery environment.
eg: RSL complements RTO and RPO as the third recovery requirement from the BIA.

def: Read-through or checklist review, tabletop discussion, walkthrough, simulation, parallel test at the recovery site and full interruption test, in increasing realism and risk. Results feed plan updates.
eg: Full interruption proves recovery best but risks production, so most programs mix types.

def: Building security activities into every phase of development (threat modeling in design, secure coding and review, security testing before release, patching and monitoring afterwards) rather than testing for security only at the end.
eg: The earlier a defect is found the cheaper it is to fix; 'shift left' is the standard exam answer.

def: Integrating security checks, automation and shared ownership into continuous integration and delivery pipelines so security keeps pace with frequent releases.
eg: Automated scanning gates and policy as code replace slow manual security sign-offs.

def: A structured method to find threats during design. STRIDE categorizes them as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege.
eg: Do it at design time, using data flow diagrams and trust boundaries; know which STRIDE category matches which attack.

def: A threat modeling technique that puts the attacker's goal at the root of a tree and decomposes it into the sub-goals and steps (joined by AND or OR logic) needed to reach it, so defenders can see the cheapest or likeliest attack paths.
eg: Another model alongside STRIDE and PASTA; the exam asks you to match method to purpose, not to run them in detail.

def: A regularly updated awareness list of the most critical web application security risks, such as broken access control, injection and cryptographic failures.
eg: It is a list of risk categories, not a standard to certify against; broken access control tops recent editions.

def: Analyzing source code or binaries without running them to find coding flaws early in development.
eg: Early and cheap but produces false positives and cannot see runtime or configuration issues.

def: Testing a running application from the outside by sending crafted requests to find exploitable behavior.
eg: Finds runtime and configuration flaws without source access; needs a deployed environment and is later in the cycle.

term: Interactive application security testing (IAST) and runtime application self-protection (RASP)
def: IAST instruments a running application during testing to report vulnerabilities with code context; RASP embeds protection inside the application to detect and block attacks at runtime.
prompt: _____ instruments a running application during testing to report vulnerabilities with code context; _____ embeds protection inside the application to detect and block attacks at runtime.
eg: IAST is a testing technique; RASP is a runtime defense. Do not confuse them with SAST and DAST.

def: SCA finds known vulnerabilities and license issues in third-party libraries; a software bill of materials lists every component in a build so exposure can be assessed quickly when a flaw is announced.
prompt: _____ finds known vulnerabilities and license issues in third-party libraries; a software bill of materials lists every component in a build so exposure can be assessed quickly when a flaw is announced.
eg: Most modern applications are mostly third-party code, so supply-chain visibility is a core cloud application control.

def: Protecting the code, dependencies, build systems and artifacts that produce software, using signed commits and artifacts, provenance records, locked dependency versions and hardened build pipelines.
eg: Attackers target build pipelines and public packages; signing and provenance prove an artifact came from your trusted build.

def: Securing programmatic interfaces with strong authentication and authorization on every call, input and schema validation, rate limiting, encryption in transit and an API gateway that centralizes policy.
eg: Broken object-level authorization is the leading API risk; inventory shadow and deprecated APIs.

def: A filter in front of web applications that inspects HTTP traffic and blocks common attacks such as injection and cross-site scripting.
eg: A compensating control that buys time; it does not replace fixing the vulnerable code.

def: Treat all input as untrusted, validate it against an allow-list, and encode output for its context so injected content is displayed as data rather than executed.
eg: The root fix for injection and cross-site scripting; blocklists are weak.

def: An attack on applications built on large language models in which crafted input, or content the model retrieves, overrides the developer's instructions and causes disclosure or unwanted actions.
eg: Defend by treating model output as untrusted, restricting tool permissions, filtering input and output and keeping secrets out of prompts.

def: Apply least privilege to model tools and data connectors, validate and sanitize model output before it reaches other systems, log prompts and responses and guard against data leakage and over-reliance on model decisions.
eg: Newer outline content; tie it to familiar principles such as input validation, authorization and monitoring.

def: Attackers query a deployed model to infer whether specific records were in its training data, reconstruct sensitive attributes or copy the model's behavior.
eg: Mitigate with rate limiting, access control, output limits and privacy-preserving training.

term: Penetration testing and vulnerability management in the cloud
def: Testing needs authorization within the provider's rules of engagement; findings flow into a managed process of prioritizing by risk, remediating and verifying.
eg: Never test provider infrastructure without permission; customer-controlled layers are generally allowed within published policy.

def: Many small services communicate over the network, so each needs authentication, authorization and encryption; a service mesh can enforce mutual TLS and policy between services.
eg: More endpoints mean a larger attack surface; zero trust between services is the cloud-native answer.

term: Identity and access management (IAM) for cloud
def: The processes and technology for establishing identities, authenticating them, authorizing access to resources and auditing activity, for people and for workloads.
eg: Identity is the primary control plane in cloud; most exam scenarios are won by stronger identity, not stronger network.

def: Trust between an identity provider and relying services lets users authenticate once and access many systems without separate credentials, with the provider issuing signed assertions or tokens.
eg: Federation centralizes authentication and deprovisioning; compromise of the identity provider has broad impact.

def: SAML exchanges XML assertions for enterprise web single sign-on; OpenID Connect adds an authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 using JSON tokens; OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization to access resources without sharing passwords.
eg: OAuth is authorization, not authentication; OpenID Connect is the authentication layer.

def: Requiring two or more independent factors: something you know, have or are. Phishing-resistant methods such as hardware security keys and passkeys are strongest.
eg: SMS codes are weaker than authenticator apps or hardware keys; privileged and remote access always need MFA.

def: RBAC grants permissions through roles tied to job function; ABAC decides using attributes of user, resource and context, allowing finer and more dynamic policy.
eg: ABAC scales better for dynamic cloud environments but is harder to audit; RBAC is simpler and common.

term: Privileged access management and just-in-time access
def: Controls for powerful accounts: vaulting credentials, session recording and granting elevated rights only for a limited approved period.
eg: Standing administrator rights are the risk; time-bound elevation shrinks the exposure window.

def: Non-human identities that applications and automation use to call services, ideally issued short-lived credentials by the platform instead of long-lived static keys.
eg: Leaked static keys are a leading breach cause; prefer role assumption and managed identities.

term: Least privilege and separation of duties
def: Give each identity only the permissions needed, and split critical tasks so no single person can complete a sensitive action alone.
eg: Expect the answer that removes excess entitlements and enforces review of who can approve and who can execute.

def: Automated creation, update and removal of accounts across systems (the System for Cross-domain Identity Management standard is common) so access follows joiner, mover and leaver events.
eg: Orphaned accounts after departures are a frequent finding; automate deprovisioning.

def: A control point between users and cloud services that provides visibility, data protection, threat detection and policy enforcement for sanctioned and unsanctioned services.
eg: Answers shadow IT and data-movement scenarios; works through API connections or proxy placement.

def: In order: broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, authentication failures, software or data integrity failures, security logging and alerting failures, and mishandling of exceptional conditions.
eg: The 2025 edition added supply chain failures and exceptional conditions; broken access control stays first. It is an awareness list, not a pass mark.

def: A catalog of verifiable security requirements for web applications and services, grouped by topic and by three assurance levels, used to specify what to build and what to test. Version 5.0 is the current release.
eg: Use ASVS to turn 'be secure' into testable requirements, and the Top 10 to raise awareness.

def: Broken object level authorization, broken authentication, broken object property level authorization, unrestricted resource consumption, broken function level authorization, unrestricted access to sensitive business flows, server-side request forgery, security misconfiguration, improper inventory management and unsafe consumption of APIs.
eg: Broken object level authorization (changing an identifier to read another user's record) is first and the most common exam scenario.

def: Prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption.
eg: Map each to a control: validate output, limit agency and permissions, protect data, vet components and rate-limit.

def: An annual list of the most dangerous software weakness types such as cross-site scripting, injection and out-of-bounds writes, published by MITRE from vulnerability data and historically presented with the SANS Institute.
eg: CWE names a weakness class; CVE names a specific flaw in a product.

term: Cloud development basics and common pitfalls
def: Good cloud practice uses stateless services, configuration outside code, managed identities and infrastructure as code. Common pitfalls are hard-coded secrets, over-permissive roles, public storage, trusting client input, unpatched dependencies and logging sensitive data.
eg: Training should target these concrete mistakes, because they cause most cloud breaches.

def: Phases typically run requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance. Security requirements come from business needs, regulation and data classification, then flow into design decisions and test cases.
eg: A missing business or regulatory requirement is the cheapest defect to fix and the costliest to find late.

def: Waterfall runs phases sequentially with gates and formal reviews; agile delivers in short iterations, so security must be built into stories, definition of done and automated tests. DevOps extends this to continuous delivery.
eg: Neither is inherently more secure; security fails when it is attached to only one gate or only the end.

def: A scoring model rating threats on damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users and discoverability, used to rank threats found by modeling. It is subjective and has been largely replaced by other scoring schemes.
eg: STRIDE finds threat types; DREAD ranks them.

def: Architecture, threats, attack surfaces and mitigations: understand the architecture, list credible threats, map where attackers can reach it and choose mitigations for each surface.
eg: It starts from architecture and attack surface rather than from a list of threat categories.

def: The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis is a seven-stage, risk-centric method that links business objectives, technical scope, application decomposition, threat analysis, vulnerability analysis, attack modeling and risk and impact analysis.
eg: Pick PASTA when the stem stresses business impact and attacker simulation.

def: The Software Assurance Forum for Excellence in Code publishes industry practices for secure development, covering design, secure coding, testing, vulnerability response and supply chain integrity.
eg: It is a practice guide from vendors; ASVS is the requirements catalog.

def: Tracking every change to code, configuration, infrastructure templates and dependencies in version control with reviews, branch protection, signed commits and tagged releases, so any build can be reproduced and traced.
eg: It underpins change control, audit and rollback.

def: Shared technology and isolation failures, provider insider threats, lack of visibility and control over the platform, legal and jurisdiction exposure and dependence on provider APIs. Design for them with encryption, logging, portability and clear data location.
eg: These risks differ from classic on-premises ones mainly in who controls the layers below the application.

def: Functional testing checks that features do what requirements say; non-functional testing checks qualities such as performance, availability, scalability and security. Both run in continuous integration and delivery pipelines.
eg: Security testing is non-functional, so a feature that passes functional tests can still be exploitable.

def: Black-box testers have no knowledge of internals and attack from outside; white-box testers have source code and design; gray-box testers have partial knowledge such as credentials or an architecture diagram.
eg: SAST is a white-box technique and DAST is a black-box technique.

term: Quality assurance and secure code review
def: Quality assurance verifies that software meets requirements before release, including security acceptance criteria. Peer and tool-assisted code review catch flaws early and spread secure coding knowledge.
eg: QA should include negative tests, not just happy paths.

def: Writing and testing scenarios of how an attacker or careless user would misuse a feature, for example enumerating identifiers, replaying a coupon or flooding a reset endpoint, as the counterpart of use cases.
eg: Abuse cases come from threat modeling and become automated negative tests.

def: Pipelines hold powerful credentials and build the code that runs in production. Protect them with least-privilege short-lived credentials, protected branches, isolated build agents, secret scanning, signed artifacts and automated security gates.
eg: A compromised pipeline defeats every downstream control.

def: Inventory every external component and service, assess the vendor, review license and support terms, track vulnerabilities, restrict what the component can access and plan for its replacement or withdrawal.
eg: You inherit the risk of what you integrate; contracts and monitoring must say who fixes what.

def: Use open-source components from trusted registries, pin and verify versions and hashes, check maintainer health and license terms, scan with software composition analysis and keep an internal mirror of approved packages.
eg: Copyleft licenses can impose obligations on your code; legal review belongs in the intake.

def: Signing builds and recording provenance proves what was built, from which source and by which pipeline. Frameworks such as SLSA define levels of build integrity, and verification at deploy time blocks unsigned or tampered artifacts.
eg: Integrity and authenticity are the two supply chain properties the outline names.

def: A gateway that inspects XML and SOAP traffic, validating schemas and blocking malformed or oversized messages and attacks such as XML external entity injection before they reach the service.
eg: Think of it as a specialized web application firewall for XML messages.

def: A front door for APIs that authenticates callers, enforces authorization, rate limits, validates requests, terminates TLS and logs traffic, giving one place to apply policy and measure use.
eg: It enforces policy at the edge; the service still needs its own authorization checks.

def: Running code in a restricted environment, such as a container, virtual machine or language runtime with limited permissions, so a compromise or untrusted file cannot affect the host or other workloads.
eg: Sandboxes are used for malware analysis, third-party plug-ins and untrusted uploads.

def: Containers package an application with its dependencies; Docker builds and runs them and Kubernetes orchestrates scheduling, scaling and networking. Security work covers image provenance, runtime restrictions, secrets handling, cluster access and network policy.
eg: The orchestrator's control plane is as sensitive as the management plane of the cloud itself.

term: Load balancers and cryptography in application architecture
def: Load balancers distribute traffic, hide back-end addresses and often terminate TLS, so certificate and cipher policy live there. Applications should use vetted libraries and managed key services rather than custom cryptography.
eg: Decide where TLS terminates and whether traffic behind the balancer is re-encrypted.

term: Identity provider and service provider trust
def: The identity provider authenticates users and issues signed assertions or tokens; the service provider (the application) trusts the provider's signature through metadata and certificates. Federation moves credentials out of each application.
eg: Compromise of the identity provider or its signing key compromises every federated application.

term: User, privileged and service access in cloud design
def: User access covers workforce and customer identities; privileged access needs stronger controls such as just-in-time elevation and session recording; service access gives workloads their own identities with short-lived credentials.
eg: Treat the three classes separately: they carry different risk and need different controls.

def: Key sources include management-plane audit logs (who did what through the console and APIs), network flow logs, operating system and application logs, identity provider logs and managed-service logs, all sent to a central protected store.
eg: Turn on management-plane logging first; without it you cannot reconstruct an account compromise.

def: A platform that collects, normalizes and correlates logs from many sources, raises alerts on suspicious patterns and retains data for investigation and compliance.
eg: Correlation and retention are the value; a SIEM fed incomplete or unsynchronized logs gives false comfort.

def: Tools that automate repetitive response tasks and orchestrate playbooks across security and IT systems, such as enriching an alert and isolating a host.
eg: SIEM detects; SOAR responds. Automate containment of high-confidence, low-impact actions and keep humans in the loop for risky ones.

def: Logs should be sent off the system that produced them, protected against tampering, time-synchronized and retained according to legal and investigative needs.
eg: Attackers delete local logs first; write-once central storage preserves evidence.

def: Continuously checks cloud configurations against benchmarks and policy, flags misconfigurations such as public storage or open management ports and can trigger remediation.
eg: Misconfiguration, not exotic exploits, causes most cloud breaches, so CSPM is a staple answer.

term: Cloud workload protection and runtime security
def: Agent or agentless tooling that monitors running workloads, containers and functions for vulnerabilities, malware and anomalous behavior.
eg: Complements posture checks: CSPM looks at configuration, workload protection looks at what is running.

def: A baseline is the approved secure configuration; drift is any deviation from it over time, detected automatically and corrected or investigated.
eg: Pairs with infrastructure as code: the template is the source of truth, and out-of-band changes are drift.

def: A controlled process for requesting, reviewing, approving, testing, implementing and recording changes so they do not introduce unmanaged risk.
eg: Emergency changes still need after-the-fact review; unauthorized change is a top cause of outages and incidents.

def: Prioritize patches by risk, test, deploy and verify. The customer patches guest operating systems and applications in IaaS; the provider patches the platform layers it operates.
eg: Know whose patch it is under each service model; unknown or unowned assets are never patched.

def: Reducing attack surface by removing unneeded services, closing ports, applying secure benchmarks and setting strong defaults on every image and instance.
eg: Harden the image once and deploy it many times; benchmark checks should be automated.

def: Regularly scanning assets, preferably with authenticated scans, then triaging by exploitability and business impact, remediating and verifying the fix.
eg: Scanning finds issues; management is the full cycle. Prioritize by risk, not by raw score alone.

def: The classic four phases are preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity (SP 800-61 Rev. 2). Rev. 3 (2025) replaces the phase model by aligning incident response with the functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0.
eg: Preparation (plans, tooling, contacts, logging) is what makes the other phases possible; containment precedes eradication.

def: Ephemeral resources vanish quickly, logs may belong to the provider, responsibilities are split and access to evidence depends on contracts, so customers must prepare in advance with logging, snapshots and provider contacts.
eg: Questions reward answers that build capability beforehand rather than improvising mid-incident.

def: Limiting the damage by isolating affected resources, for example moving an instance to a quarantine security group, revoking credentials and snapshotting storage, rather than powering it off and destroying volatile evidence.
eg: Preserve evidence while stopping spread; revoke or rotate compromised credentials immediately.

def: Collecting, preserving and analyzing evidence such as disk snapshots, memory captures and logs in a way that keeps its integrity and admissibility, within the limits of access the provider allows.
eg: Work on copies, hash evidence, document everything and know what the provider can supply under contract.

def: A documented record of who collected, handled, stored and transferred evidence, with times and purpose, proving it has not been altered.
eg: A broken chain of custody can make evidence inadmissible, however good the analysis.

def: Collect the most short-lived evidence first: memory and running processes, then network connections, then disk and storage, then remote logs and archival media.
eg: In cloud, snapshot memory and volumes before terminating an instance, because the instance may not exist later.

def: Preparing in advance to collect evidence quickly: enabling logs, defining retention, setting up isolated analysis accounts, tooling and legal and contractual arrangements with the provider.
eg: The cloud equivalent of preparation in the incident life cycle.

def: The team and processes that monitor, triage and respond to security events. Useful metrics include mean time to detect and mean time to respond.
eg: Measure outcomes over time; alert volume alone says nothing about effectiveness.

def: Documented, step-by-step procedures for handling specific incident types or operations, increasingly automated, so response is consistent and fast.
eg: Test them in exercises; an untested playbook fails when needed.

def: Threat intelligence provides context on adversaries and indicators; threat hunting proactively searches for undetected compromise using hypotheses, and increasingly uses machine learning to find anomalies.
eg: Hunting assumes the attacker is already in; the revised outline highlights AI and ML as hunting tools.

def: Analytics that build baselines of normal behavior for users and systems and flag deviations, such as impossible travel or unusual data downloads.
eg: Useful for detecting stolen credentials and insider abuse where no signature exists.

term: Model drift as a security signal
def: A deployed machine learning model whose behavior shifts over time without an intentional update may indicate data poisoning, tampering or changed input patterns, so model performance should be monitored like any other control.
eg: New AI-related operations content: monitor models for unexpected change and investigate it as a potential incident.

term: Intrusion detection and prevention in the cloud
def: Network and host based tools, plus provider-native threat detection, that identify and optionally block malicious activity; virtual appliances and traffic mirroring supply the visibility physical taps once gave.
eg: Encrypted traffic limits network inspection; host and identity telemetry fill the gap.

def: Operations practices from frameworks such as ITIL and ISO/IEC 20000 (incident, problem, change, release, configuration and availability management) feed continual service improvement.
eg: Security operations must integrate with these processes, not sit beside them.

def: A communication plan names who informs executives, legal counsel, regulators, customers and the provider, with timelines driven by law and contract.
eg: Legal and compliance teams decide what is disclosed and when; technical staff do not improvise public statements.

def: Operating across several providers requires a normalized log schema, centralized detection, consistent identity and runbooks that account for each provider's tools and evidence limits.
eg: A stated emphasis of the newer outline: tool sprawl and inconsistent visibility are the main risks.

def: Standing up infrastructure with safe initial settings: deny-by-default networking, encryption on, unneeded services and ports off, default credentials removed and logging enabled, enforced by hardened images and policy.
eg: Defaults should be the secure state so a forgotten setting never exposes anything.

term: Hardware security configuration: HSM and TPM
def: A hardware security module holds keys and performs cryptography in tamper-resistant hardware, so it needs access policy, firmware control and backup of key material. A trusted platform module anchors measured boot and remote attestation on a host, and must be enabled and provisioned.
eg: Know which one stores customer keys (HSM) and which one attests host integrity (TPM).

term: Management plane tools: installation and configuration
def: Tools that provision and control the environment (consoles, command-line interfaces, orchestration and automation) need hardened hosts, multi-factor authentication, least-privilege roles, signed and current software and complete audit logging.
eg: Install them on controlled administrative hosts, never on personal machines.

def: Harden virtual networks (segmentation and separate management networks), storage (encryption and access control), memory (no overcommit for sensitive tenants, guarded sharing) and CPU settings, and choose hypervisor type deliberately: Type 1 for production, Type 2 mainly on workstations.
eg: Disable unused virtual devices such as floppy, serial and clipboard sharing to shrink the attack surface.

def: Integration software installed in a guest, such as VMware Tools, Hyper-V integration services or cloud-init agents, improves drivers, time sync, shutdown and monitoring. It runs with high privilege and must be patched, trusted and sourced from the vendor.
eg: An outdated toolset is an attack path between guest and hypervisor.

term: Remote access: bastions, jump hosts and consoles
def: Administrative access should pass through a hardened bastion or jump host, use SSH keys or certificates and multi-factor authentication, restrict RDP to the bastion, prefer session-managed or console access without open inbound ports, and record sessions.
eg: Exposing RDP or SSH directly to the internet is the classic finding.

def: A VLAN divides one physical network into separate broadcast domains using tags, separating tenants, tiers or management traffic. VLANs are not encryption and misconfigured trunks allow VLAN hopping.
prompt: A _____ divides one physical network into separate broadcast domains using tags, separating tenants, tiers or management traffic. _____ are not encryption and misconfigured trunks allow _____ hopping.
eg: Combine VLANs with firewall rules and, in clouds, with virtual network constructs.

def: Rogue DHCP servers can hand out malicious gateways and resolvers, and clients can exhaust address pools. Controls include DHCP snooping on switches, port security and monitoring of lease logs.
eg: In public cloud the provider runs address assignment, but virtual networks you build still need the control.

def: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify that answers are authentic and unmodified. It gives integrity and origin authentication but not confidentiality.
